items.prompt: How does this unit define "inheritance"?
choices: An object built by combining smaller, independent parts

A way to store data in a database
A method for encrypting class properties

🌳 Inheritance — "is-a," one parent, tree-shaped
🧩 Composition — "has-a," independent parts combined
items.explanation: Inheritance models an "is-a" relationship — a subclass extends a parent class, reusing and optionally overriding its behavior. It works cleanly for a single, stable axis of variation.

items.prompt: What kind of relationship does inheritance model well, per this unit?
choices: A "has-a" relationship between independent parts
A single, stable "is-a" relationship with one axis of variation
A relationship between two completely unrelated classes
A relationship that always requires multiple inheritance
items.reference:
🌳 Inheritance — "is-a," one parent, tree-shaped
🧩 Composition — "has-a," independent parts combined
items.explanation: Inheritance fits cleanly when a category genuinely has a single, stable axis of variation — a subclass picks exactly one branch of the tree, which works as long as there's only one dimension to branch along.

items.prompt: How does this unit define "composition"?
choices: A subclass extending a parent class

A way to compile multiple classes into one file

items.reference:
🌳 Inheritance — "is-a," one parent, tree-shaped
🧩 Composition — "has-a," independent parts combined
items.explanation: Composition models a "has-a" relationship — an object is built by combining smaller, independent pieces, each handling one concern, assembled together rather than inherited from a single parent.

items.prompt: What's the key structural advantage composition has over inheritance for combining independent capabilities?
choices: Composition requires fewer lines of code in every single case
Composition doesn't limit an object to a single instance of a given kind of part, unlike a tree where a subclass can only extend one parent
Composition automatically generates documentation
Composition is always faster at runtime than inheritance
items.reference:
🌳 Inheritance — "is-a," one parent, tree-shaped
🧩 Composition — "has-a," independent parts combined
items.explanation: Composition doesn't restrict an object to a single instance of a given kind of part — nothing about "has-a" limits a character to exactly one attack behavior, unlike single inheritance's one-parent-only constraint.

items.prompt: What is "combinatorial explosion", as this unit defines it?
choices: A bug that causes a program to crash unexpectedly
When two or more independent axes of variation are each modeled as separate class hierarchies, the number of classes needed to cover every combination grows multiplicatively
A technique for compressing large codebases
A term for when a class has too many private fields
items.reference:
📈 Combinatorial explosion — classes multiply, not add
🧮 n move styles × m attack styles = n×m subclasses
items.explanation: Combinatorial explosion happens when independent axes of variation (like movement style and attack style) are each modeled as separate class hierarchies — the number of classes needed to cover every combination grows multiplicatively, not additively.

items.prompt: If a design has 4 movement styles and 4 attack styles, and each combination needs its own subclass, how many subclasses does combinatorial explosion predict are needed?

1, since a single base class can cover everything
items.reference:

🧮 n move styles × m attack styles = n×m subclasses
items.explanation: Combinatorial explosion is multiplicative: 4 movement styles × 4 attack styles = 16 subclasses needed to cover every combination if each is modeled as its own class, versus just 8 components under composition (4 + 4).
